title: First, remember the Power
hookLine: the opening lines, from the Tenth Guru's Chandi di Var, remember the Divine as Bhagauti, the power of the sword

lines: THE ARDAS STARTS THE SAME WAY.
cards: Before a sprinter settles into the blocks, there's a moment where she isn't thinking about the race at all. She's gathering something.
Before a surgeon makes the first cut, before a firefighter goes up the ladder, there's that same breath. Not a plan. A summoning of strength from somewhere deeper than the plan.

The Ardas has a moment like that right at its start. After the greeting, before naming a single Guru, it remembers a power. And the word it uses for that power has been argued over by readers for a long time.

teach.b: The lines come from a poem by Guru Gobind Singh, the Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, also called Chandi di Var, the ballad of Chandi. Its first stanza begins: pritham bhagauti simar kai, guru nanak laeen dhiai.
In paraphrase: first, remember Bhagauti, then turn your mind to Guru Nanak. So the order of the whole Ardas starts here: first the Power, then the Gurus. Now, that word.
In Punjabi, a bhagauti can be a sword.

teach.h: BHAGAUTI: THE SWORD, GOD AS POWER.
teach.b: Because of that, Sikh readers understand Bhagauti here as God seen as power: the Timeless One whose strength cuts through injustice and fear, with the sword as its sign.
The Khalsa's double-edged khanda and the kirpan carry the same idea.

Other readers notice that the ballad goes on to tell the battles of the goddess Chandi from old Indian tales, and they hear Bhagauti as the goddess. Sikh teaching, and the way the Ardas is prayed, hold to the one God.
Scholars also discuss how the Dasam Granth's poems were compiled. The words of the line, though, are the same for everyone: first, remember. Why put power first, before the Gurus, before any request?
One answer Sikhs give: the Ardas is said by a community that has needed courage, under persecution, on battlefields, in prisons.
Starting with the Power reminds the one praying that strength isn't something they have to manufacture.
It's something to remember, the way a sprinter remembers what her legs can do. And there's a quiet humility in it: you begin a prayer not with yourself, but with what's greater than you.

how: Every Ardas opens with the first stanza of Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, remembering Bhagauti and then the Gurus; Sikhs say it standing, often in a strong, rhythmic voice.

o: the first Guru's name for the Creator
the sword, and God seen as power
a hymn sung before the battle begins

games.q: you're about to pray the Ardas for a friend in trouble. by its opening line, what comes first?
o: a list of what you've done right.
games.why: pritham bhagauti simar kai: first remember the Power, then the Gurus, and only later the request.

practice: Sit tall, feet flat on the floor, and notice where strength already lives in you: your spine holding you up, your lungs filling without being asked.
You didn't make any of that; let yourself remember it, the way the Ardas remembers before it asks. If you pray, say Waheguru on each out-breath, as a way of remembering where the strength comes from.

wordCard.voice: Bhagauti. The sword, and the Power it stands for: in the Ardas, God remembered first, before anything is asked.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Bhagauti, a sword, and in the Ardas, God remembered as power.

carryVoice: Your line: first, remember. Strength is something you remember, not something you make. Until tomorrow.
